summary: Bennett Fenner, a Rust developer at Zed, demonstrates building an ACP-compatible coding agent live in TypeScript. Zed built an AI code editor in Rust and, responding to the rise of AI coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI, developed ACP (Agent Client Protocol) — a JSON RPC-based protocol similar to MCP and LSP that lets agents and clients communicate through a unified interface. ACP is open source, with 40+ clients (including JetBrains, Obsidian, Open Claw) and agents like Open Code and Cursor supporting it natively or via adapters. The session begins with a pre-existing minimal coding agent in TypeScript with two tools: read_file and edit_file. The agent uses the Anthropic API and follows the standard agent loop — sending conversation context to the stateless model API, receiving either an end-turn message or tool calls, executing tool calls locally, and feeding results back. To make this ACP-compatible, Bennett implements the agent interface from the TypeScript SDK, requiring four functions: initialize (respond with protocol version and capabilities), session new (generate random session ID, instantiate agent with working directory), prompt (look up agent by session ID, extract text from content blocks, call agent prompt function), and cancellation. The agent is registered in Zed by pointing to the agent.js file run with Node. Streaming is implemented by passing the ACP connection to the coding agent, using Anthropic SDK stream events to send session updates — notifications containing agent message chunks that the client renders as streaming text. For tool calls, the agent emits an initial tool call session update with in-progress status, then a tool call update with results upon completion. Bennett also demonstrates ACP's file system proxying capability, where the client provides file system access, enabling editors to share unsaved buffer changes with agents. In the final segment, Bennett bootstraps the agent to add a terminal tool to itself by leveraging its file read/write capabilities. ACP also supports a terminal management capability where clients can create and manage terminals for agents. The live demo shows the self-modified agent successfully running a terminal command (sleep 5, ls) in Zed. During Q&A, Bennett explains that ACP supports multiple content types including diffs, where the agent sends old text and new text and Zed performs the diffing. He also confirms the connection works over standard IO, with JetBrains folks working on remote transport support. The entire implementation took approximately 15 minutes. The demo code is available at agentclientprotocol.com but should not be used in production as it is agent-generated.

sections.title: Introduction to ACP and Zed
sections.summary: Bennett introduces himself as a Zed developer who built an AI code editor in Rust. He explains that with the rise of AI coding agents, Zed needed a protocol to let users bring any agent into a unified interface, leading to ACP — a JSON RPC-based protocol similar to MCP and LSP. ACP is open source with 40+ clients and multiple agents supporting it natively or via adapters.

sections.title: Pre-existing coding agent overview
sections.summary: Bennett shows a minimal TypeScript coding agent with read_file and edit_file tools using the Anthropic API. He explains the standard agent loop: send conversation context to the stateless model API, receive either an end-turn message or tool calls, execute tool calls locally, and feed results back. The handle_tool_call function manages reading and writing files.

sections.title: Implementing ACP interface and first demo
sections.summary: Bennett implements the ACP agent interface from the TypeScript SDK, requiring four functions: initialize (protocol version and capabilities), session new (random session ID, instantiate agent with working directory, store in internal map), prompt (look up agent by session ID, extract text, call prompt function), and cancellation. The agent is registered in Zed by pointing to agent.js run with Node. First demo shows Zed sending session new and prompt requests but no token output yet.

sections.title: Streaming tokens via session updates
sections.summary: Bennett passes the ACP connection and session ID to the coding agent, then uses Anthropic SDK stream events to send session updates — notifications containing agent message chunks. These asynchronous updates let the client render streaming text. Demo shows streaming working with Opus output appearing in Zed chunk by chunk.

sections.title: Tool call updates and file system proxying
sections.summary: Bennett implements tool call session updates: an initial update with in-progress status and metadata, then a completion update with content. He also switches from native fs.readFile to ACP's read_text_file, proxying file system operations through the client so editors can share unsaved buffer changes. Demo shows read and edit tool calls appearing in Zed with diffs, though a duplication bug and connection issues appear near the end without time to debug.

sections.title: Self-bootstrapping terminal tool and Q&A
sections.summary: Bennett bootstraps the agent by asking it to add a terminal tool to itself using its file read/write capabilities. He explains ACP's terminal management capability where clients can create and manage terminals for agents. The agent generates a new tool description, the code builds successfully, and the demo shows the terminal running 'sleep 5' and 'ls' with output visible in Zed. Bennett wraps up noting the implementation took about 15 minutes and points to agentclientprotocol.com for the demo code (not for production). During Q&A, he explains ACP supports multiple content types including diffs where the agent sends old text and new text and Zed does the diffing. He confirms connections work over standard IO with remote transport in development by JetBrains.
